material_culture.description: Raised wooden and bamboo architecture built on hardwood piles 6-8 feet above ground level to withstand monsoon flooding from the Buridihing and keep out wild animals. The open area below (tai3 hɯn1) is used for weaving looms and keeping livestock.

material_culture.lik_tai: သၢဝ်မႆႉလွင်
material_culture.english_name: master center pillar of stilted house
material_culture.description: The sacred central post of the Khamyang home, ritually erected during house construction with offerings to the guardian spirits of the dwelling (phi5 hɯn1).
Central clay-lined earth box hearth suspended on the bamboo floor. Serves as the spiritual center of the family where food is cooked and tea is shared with guests.
Wooden handloom operated beneath the stilted house where Khamyang women weave intricate geometric textiles, shoulder bags (tung1), and traditional lungis.
Distinctive dark cotton or silk waist-cloth woven with horizontal stripes, worn by Tai Khamyang women on ceremonial and monastic occasions.

material_culture.lik_tai: ၶျွၵ်းတမ်ၶဝ်ႈ
material_culture.english_name: wooden foot-pestle and mortar for husking rice
material_culture.description: Heavy wooden treadle-pestle operated by foot lever to dehusk paddy and crush rice into fine powder for festive rice cakes.
Horizontal frame loom constructed from hardwood and bamboo, used by Tai Khamyang women to weave patterned silk and cotton textiles.
material_culture.cultural_significance: Weaving is considered a core cultural virtue; every home in Powaimukh retains a dedicated loom area under or beside the stilt house.

material_culture.description: Massive hollowed-log drum covered with stretched cowhide, suspended in the monastery drum tower.
material_culture.cultural_significance: Beaten at dawn and dusk to signal monk chanting hours and summon villagers for communal assemblies.

material_culture.description: Tightly woven conical bamboo basket placed in flowing streams and river shallows of the Buridihing to catch fish and river prawns.
material_culture.cultural_significance: Reflects deep traditional ecological knowledge of aquatic currents and seasonal fish migration.

ethnobotany_and_fauna.description: Primary staple crop of the Tai Khamyang. Cultivated in flooded alluvial wetlands (naa1). Varieties include sticky winter rice (khaw3 niew1) and dry rice.
Cultivated climbing creeper whose aromatic leaves are essential for hospitality, wedding ritual trays (phan1), and monastic offerings.
Tall slender palm producing areca nuts chewed with betel leaf. Chewed during social gatherings as an etiquette of respect.
Climbing rattan cane abundant along local rivers. Gives Powaimukh its historical name: 'Maan3 Paa1 Waai6' (Village at the River-Mouth of Rattan). Used for sturdy basketry and ropes.
Vital draft animal in Khamyang wet-rice tillage. Featured prominently in moral folklore (e.g. Lik Pung: Kwaai1 Kap4 Sɯa1).
Revered wildlife of the rainforests flanking the Patkai mountains. Historically captured and trained by Tai masters for timber work.
Apex predator of Upper Assam jungles; figures in traditional wisdom stories contrasting physical ferocity with animal intelligence.
Revered bird in Tai Buddhist art and iconography, symbolizing beauty and spiritual vigilance.

festivals_and_rituals.description: The paramount religious festival of the Tai Khamyang. Lasting 3 days, villagers take the Buddha statues from the monastery, erect a temporary pavilion (kyong1 phraa4), and pour consecrated water (song1 nam4 phraa4) to cleanse misfortune and welcome the new year.
Tai Buddhist festival of offering firewood to the monastery. Youths construct an elaborate hexagonal wooden tower of fuel timber and burn it at dawn to symbolically warm the Lord Buddha.
Ceremony of consecrating and donating a newly sculpted Buddha image or sacred Lik Tai manuscript to the village temple.

festivals_and_rituals.lik_tai: မေႇလမ်မေႇၽီ
festivals_and_rituals.description: Ancient ancestral worship ceremony honoring the departed spirits of forefathers (Dam) and celestial deities (Phi) for community peace and fertility.

festivals_and_rituals.lik_tai: ပွႆးၵထိၼ်ႇ
festivals_and_rituals.description: Major post-rainy season Buddhist festival where villagers jointly weave, sew, and offer sacred saffron robes to the monastic Sangha.
festivals_and_rituals.cultural_significance: Highest communal merit-making festival of the Buddhist year in Powaimukh.

festivals_and_rituals.description: Ceremonial festival celebrating the copying, donation, and public recitation of palm-leaf and sanchi-bark manuscripts (Lik Tai).
festivals_and_rituals.cultural_significance: Crucial ritual mechanism through which Tai Buddhist literature was historically preserved and transmitted across centuries.
